analysis.one_liner: Bans agreements between employers not to hire each other's workers.
analysis.headline: The bill would have outlawed employer agreements that restrict hiring, but it never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Some companies agree with each other — formally or informally — not to hire away each other's employees, sometimes through franchise contracts. That leaves workers with fewer outside offers and less leverage to bargain for raises. This bill would declare such agreements illegal, treating them like price-fixing under the antitrust laws, with penalties under the Sherman Act and the FTC Act. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its antitrust subcommittee and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies that use or could use these 'no-poach' agreements, especially franchise employees, whose potential outside job offers shrink when employers agree not to hire each other's staff. Removing the agreements would make it easier to get competing offers and negotiate higher pay.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any employer to enter into, enforce, or threaten to enforce an agreement that prohibits or restricts hiring or soliciting another employer's current or former employees, including agreements embedded in franchise and contractor contracts [S3].

Treats violations as contracts in restraint of trade under the Sherman Act and unfair methods of competition under the FTC Act, giving the government and workers the same legal tools used against price-fixing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large employers and franchise brands that rely on no-poach and no-solicitation clauses to hold down turnover and wage competition would lose a tool they currently use, and would face antitrust liability if they kept using them.

drawbacks.text: No-poach clauses are sometimes justified as protecting a franchisor's investment in training franchisee employees or guarding trade secrets; an outright ban gives employers no narrower alternative to protect those interests.
The bill covers agreements between any two employers, without a size threshold, so even small businesses agreeing to informal no-hiring understandings would face Sherman Act exposure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — restoring job mobility and wage competition for workers — is broad and well-documented in antitrust economics; no-poach agreements function like wage-fixing among employers. The main cost falls on employers who currently use these clauses, and a blanket ban is a blunt instrument compared with narrower rules protecting training investments. The honest cost is modest relative to the wage gains for workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its antitrust subcommittee in 2019, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on July 23, 2019, joined by Rep. David Cicilline as its sole cosponsor [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced, and on August 15, 2019 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's record: it never received a committee hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who use no-poach and no-solicitation clauses — particularly franchise brands — kept a tool that limits workers' outside job offers, because the bill never advanced far enough to threaten it.

industries.note: Franchise contracts have been a common vehicle for no-poach clauses binding franchisees not to hire each other's workers. The bill would expressly cover agreements made through franchise agreements and impose Sherman Act liability for keeping them, removing a tool that limits workers' outside offers and wage bargaining.

industries.industry: Large employers and staffing chains generally
industries.note: Any two employers agreeing not to solicit or hire each other's employees — a practice used to reduce turnover and hold down wage competition — would face antitrust penalties. Workers lose outside offers under these agreements, so the industry's interest in keeping them runs against workers' pay.
